speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Deputy Speaker, Sir, the Workers' Party (WP) has mooted the idea of a redundancy insurance scheme for some time now.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We raised it in our manifestoes for the General Elections in 2011 and 2015, and the hon Member Ms Sylvia Lim raised it in the Budget Debate in 2016.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Party published a fleshed-out proposal in November last year, followed by a modest public consultation exercise to gather feedback.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We are encouraged by the feedback, and thankful to members of the public for their invaluable contributions, which have highlighted the pros and cons of our redundancy insurance scheme proposal.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The first principle is to generate risk-pooling to reduce the financial pressure on workers who are made redundant.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The second principle is to reduce insecurity and worry among the vast majority of employed Singaporeans.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The third principle is to complement the existing programmes targeting the retraining and re-employment of workers under the Adapt and Grow initiative.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The first principle is to establish a system of progressive risk-pooling to reduce the financial pressure that workers experience when they are made redundant.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The risk of being made redundant increases with age, though we are now witnessing a greater proportion of younger workers being laid off.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Nevertheless, older workers, particularly those aged 40 and above, tend to face a triple whammy, compared to younger workers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Older workers face a greater risk of being made redundant.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: They also face the intergenerational squeeze and have more bills to pay.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Financial pressure points include children's education, support for elderly parents, as well as hefty mortgages and escalating healthcare costs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: On top of these two factors, their prospects for re-employment have historically been worse than younger workers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Growing old is a certainty in life and the younger workers would one day face the triple whammy their seniors face today.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This payout would be subject to a cap of 40% of the prevailing monthly median wage of resident workers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Based on the 2014 median gross monthly income of $3,000, excluding employer CPF contributions, a worker would receive up to a monthly payout of $1,200 for six months.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The objective here is to reduce the financial pressure felt by workers, especially older workers, when they are made redundant.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As a supplement to cash savings, the redundancy insurance payouts would give affected workers some peace of mind to look for suitable employment or to retrain and acquire new skills to make themselves relevant again in the labour market.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The intention here is to minimise the distraction of financial pressures so that affected workers would do what they should be doing in such a situation, that is, focus on getting the next job.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We should not subscribe to an either-or fallacy to downplay the usefulness of redundancy insurance.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Some dismissals of redundancy insurance apply such a fallacy.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Some have argued that redundancy insurance payouts would discourage workers from saving for rainy days.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is quite ridiculous to think that the maximum $7,200 payout that an affected worker stands to gain would discourage him or her from saving excess cash, especially in our thrifty culture.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There is no evidence to suggest that the purchase of life insurance discourages Singaporeans from saving for their loved ones.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Otherwise, why would the Government encourage lower-income Singaporeans to buy life insurance by providing for life insurance relief for personal income tax?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Another dismissal of redundancy insurance goes along the lines that there are already many Government programmes providing ample cash assistance to the needy.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Redundancy insurance payouts are not meant to replace the assistance provided to the needy.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Most workers who are made redundant do not fall into the needy category and would not need cash assistance.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Redundancy insurance aims to reduce the financial pressure faced by affected workers and the resultant distractions caused by the pressure, so that workers can focus on getting their retraining and re-employment right.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Redundancy insurance helps affected workers to find re-employment in a timely manner so that they would not need to depend on Government cash assistance.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In this sense, redundancy insurance is a preventive measure, helping affected workers to avoid the vicious poverty trap and to maintain their financial independence.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The second principle of the proposed redundancy insurance scheme is to reduce insecurity and worry among the vast majority of employed Singaporeans.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As the trend of more young workers getting affected by redundancies indicates, no one is safe from the risk of redundancy anymore.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Technological and economic disruptions, and increasing protectionist sentiments around the globe, also mean that no industry is immune to layoffs and workforce shakeups.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: During the financial crisis, redundancies peaked at the fourth quarter of 2008 and the first and second quarters of 2009 but quickly went back to the normal levels of 2,000-plus redundancies per quarter.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We are not experiencing the acute injury of an economic crisis, but the chronic pain of economic restructuring amidst global disruptions.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In this situation, all workers face massive insecurity and worry about their future.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There are two areas where the insecurities are being felt: skills mismatch and fragmentation of employment.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Redundancy insurance complements existing Government programmes to reduce the insecurity and worry.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The first area is skills mismatch, which has led to laid-off workers struggling to find re-employment.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The net psychological effects are two-fold: increasing demoralisation among laid-off workers leading to more discouraged workers and fearful workers clinging to their jobs instead of actively seeking lifelong learning.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Of course, the Government is keenly aware of this issue and has been rightly pouring resources into retraining and skills upgrading.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Redundancy insurance complements these existing efforts by providing laid-off workers with breathing space to retrain and upgrade their skills to match demand in the labour market.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is preferred to laid-off workers desperately signing on to the first job they could find, which could lead to long-term underemployment and worsen skills mismatch in the wider economy.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We propose that the subsequent redundancy insurance payouts after the first payout should be tied to the condition that the worker is either actively seeking a new job through the National Jobs Bank or is actively retraining himself through the various Government programmes.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This will ensure that redundancy insurance complements the national movement to improve skills and to minimise skills mismatch in the economy.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This will also counter the criticism that redundancy insurance would increase unemployment rates, which is highly unlikely in our proposal in the first place as the payout is deliberately kept at a conservative level and will not be a disincentive to re-employment.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The second area is the fragmentation of employment, which refers to the changing nature of work as more workers turn to freelancing and contract for service as their primary source of income.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is something that is beginning to be felt in Singapore, and Manpower Minister Lim Swee Say gave a speech on the gig economy at the Committee of Supply this year, in which he said that a tripartite workgroup is to study the issues faced by freelancers and to address them and to protect the well-being of freelancers with practical solutions.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: One of these issues is when contract workers are made redundant through the early termination of their contracts.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We propose that the redundancy insurance scheme also covers self-employed workers, and this would include entrepreneurs, in order to provide them with a safety net like employed workers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Self-employed workers will contribute 0.1% of their self-declared income to the scheme.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: One argument against redundancy insurance is that it will inadvertently increase insecurity by making employers more willing to retrench workers or give less retrenchment benefits.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But these moral hazard criticisms are only valid if employers operate in an unregulated and demoralised environment.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I find it strange the idea that employers would push workers off their buildings knowing that there is a safety net below to catch the workers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is to suggest that after so many decades of tripartite partnership, union representations and Government promotion of workers' rights, our moral economy of stable industrial relations is going to be undermined by a mere social insurance programme.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The third principle of the proposed redundancy insurance scheme is to complement the existing programmes under the Government's Adapt and Grow initiative.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As I have mentioned repeatedly, the proposed redundancy insurance scheme does not displace or replace existing programmes to help our unemployed workers and jobseekers but seeks to complement existing programmes.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: To think otherwise is to subscribe to the either-or fallacy: choose either the WP's redundancy insurance scheme or the Government's Adapt and Grow programmes.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Some commentators have framed the false choice as such: redundancy insurance is paid for by the workers themselves and the Adapt and Grow programmes by the Government.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is another either-or fallacy that encourages an entitlement mentality.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It runs against this Government's oft-stated principle of fostering resilient independence among our citizens and discouraging dependence on Government welfare schemes.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In fact, I do not only see the redundancy insurance scheme as complementing Adapt and Grow.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I see it as a very good candidate to become part of the Adapt and Grow suite of programmes to help Singaporean workers retrain and get re-employed.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And what gap can the redundancy insurance scheme plug?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Adapt and Grow initiatives can provide excellent assistance for workers who are laid off.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If they sign up with Workforce Singapore (WSG) to try out new jobs or training attachments in specific sectors, rank-and-file workers and professionals, managers, executives and technicians (PMETs), will receive allowances from the Government.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For senior PMETs who are made redundant or unemployed for six months or more, they could turn to the Career Support Programme which offers salary, training and placement support.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But these programmes work only if laid-off workers decide to turn to the Government for help in the first place.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: After many decades of cultivating a resilient and independent workforce, turning to the Government for immediate assistance on labour market endeavours after losing one's job is a foreign concept for Singaporean workers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In fact, it is a good thing that our workers are a resilient and independent bunch and prefer to try to look for a job on their own first before turning to the Government for help.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I do not think the Government disagrees with me on this, as the Career Support Programme policy for junior PMETs remain one of extending aid only if the workers have been unemployed for six months or more, regardless of whether they were made redundant.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In other words, laid-off PMETs below 40 years of age are expected to seek re-employment on their own for six months before they can receive Government assistance.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This also implies that the six months after being laid off is a crucial period where the independence and resourcefulness of our workers are applied to finding a new job before the risk of discouragement starts to escalate.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The labour market, when properly structured and regulated, should be left to its own devices to sort out supply and demand matching, but market failures should also be addressed, especially if market failures could lead to the discouragement of our workers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Six months seem to be the natural and reasonable period for laid-off workers to sort themselves out with the market, before they turn to the Government for assistance.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In this sense then, the proposed redundancy insurance scheme would fit into the Adapt and Grow initiative.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It provides a safety net for all laid-off workers, regardless of whether they choose immediate Government assistance or not.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It encourages workers to exercise their independence and resourcefulness to sort out their employment situation in the labour marketplace first and, failing which, then they can turn to Government assistance with the dignity of knowing that they have tried.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Another benefit of the redundancy insurance scheme is that it cultivates a strong social consciousness among Singaporean workers, promoting a sense of solidarity among them across skills levels, income groups and generations.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Even as each worker seeks to compete effectively in the labour market to maximise one's own interests and earn the remuneration one meritoriously deserves, each would also know by way of the redundancy insurance that all Singaporean workers are looking out for one another in case anyone is felled by redundancies that no one could have predicted or prevented.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is the promise of social insurance for our society made more vulnerable by the fragmentation of employment and global economic disruptions.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And there is psychological defence knowing that we got one another's back as we sail the waters of global uncertainty.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For redundancy insurance, sunny days are those years when redundancies stay relatively low and employment relatively high.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Many developed countries have established some form of redundancy insurance to ameliorate problems arising from their maturing economies.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Many of these redundancy insurance policies share features with the one that we have proposed here.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Programmes in Canada, France and South Korea also have the condition that affected workers are actively looking for work in order to receive the payouts.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I am not arguing that we should follow suit just because our peer economies are doing so.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There are differences in circumstances, which is why our proposed scheme adapts the basic features of redundancy insurance to our situation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But there are similar issues that point to the usefulness of redundancy insurance in addressing the issues.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As developed economies seek to boost labour productivity and innovation amidst technological disruption, structural unemployment will rise.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: At this point, I would like to make the note that the topic of unemployment insurance is not a new topic in this House.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: More recently, hon Members, such as Ms Sylvia Lim, Ms Foo Mee Har, Mr Patrick Tay and Mr Azmoon Ahmad, have brought up the idea in one form or another.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: What I have offered here is the synopsis of the fleshed-out proposal that was published by WP in November last year and additional arguments highlighting the benefits of the proposal.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Mr Patrick Tay had said in the Debate on the President's Address in January last year that unemployment insurance merits closer study and scrutiny.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Foreign Affairs and Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: That is why the priority has always been to help workers in jobs keep jobs and to help workers who lose their jobs find new jobs.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Foreign Affairs and Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: It is also why the People's Action Party (PAP) Government has never taken its eye off job creation.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Foreign Affairs and Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This approach has kept Singaporeans employed and unemployment low.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Foreign Affairs and Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: However, as our economic situation changed, and restructuring became a necessity and a concern, we have built up many schemes to help workers who lose their jobs.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Foreign Affairs and Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This is something that Assoc Prof Daniel Goh has acknowledged.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Foreign Affairs and Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We also have schemes like ComCare and bursaries that provide short-term relief to Singaporeans while they are out of a job.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Foreign Affairs and Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: There are many schemes but all with a single purpose − to get workers back at work, with new and useful skills, and to ease the transition and moderate the impact on their families.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Foreign Affairs and Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We have not hesitated to give generous wage support and training subsidies, but always conditional on the worker making the effort by attending a training course or accepting a placement opportunity.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Foreign Affairs and Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: But, as the Prime Minister and Minister Lim Swee Say have pointed out, there is still a risk that, in future, our unemployment rate will rise beyond what we have been used to.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Foreign Affairs and Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Unemployment insurance, including redundancy insurance, are not crazy ideas and neither are they new, as Assoc Prof Daniel Goh acknowledged.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Foreign Affairs and Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Indeed, many developed countries have had some form of unemployment insurance for years.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Foreign Affairs and Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: But their unemployment rates are generally significantly higher than ours.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Foreign Affairs and Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Many people in these countries can see themselves having to depend on payouts.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Foreign Affairs and Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: As a result, their attitude is, "If we have to pay premiums, so be it".

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Foreign Affairs and Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Singapore today is not in the same position.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Foreign Affairs and Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We have focused our efforts on employment support through training and reskilling, with full support from employers and unions, which other countries find harder to do.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Foreign Affairs and Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Unemployment and redundancy insurance also have their downsides, which WP has not talked about.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Foreign Affairs and Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In Denmark, studies have shown that while many jobless persons do get a job within the payout period, many more wait until just before the benefits expire to take on available jobs.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Foreign Affairs and Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In other words, the jobs are there but the unemployed workers delay taking them up.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Foreign Affairs and Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This is a real pity, because the longer a person stays out of a job, the harder it is to find work.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Foreign Affairs and Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: A second downside is that redundancy insurance is actually not cheap.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Foreign Affairs and Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: WP claims that we only need 0.1% of monthly salary, shared equally between employers and employees.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Foreign Affairs and Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: However, this is too good to be true, even based on the Member's own research findings.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Foreign Affairs and Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The Republic of Korea needs 1.35%, which is at least 10 times the Member's estimate.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Foreign Affairs and Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Today, premiums in the Republic of Korea have risen to 2.2%.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Foreign Affairs and Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: WP has not explained what is so different about its proposal that costs so much less.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Foreign Affairs and Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: That worries me, especially for our small and medium enterprises (SMEs).

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Foreign Affairs and Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Will employers offset the premiums by paying their workers lower salaries?

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Foreign Affairs and Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Will employers feel less obligation to retrain and retain, resulting in higher redundancies?

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Foreign Affairs and Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Do everything possible to help displaced workers find replacement jobs and give the displaced workers every incentive to make the effort to help themselves.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Foreign Affairs and Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This is the right strategic approach and will go a long way.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Foreign Affairs and Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: A few days before Chinese New Year in 2009, some 600 employees in one of our unionised companies were told they were being laid off.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Foreign Affairs and Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The timing was cruel and the union had not been consulted.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Foreign Affairs and Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: But we had to stay focused on helping the workers.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Foreign Affairs and Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We knew the workers were in for a tough time.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Foreign Affairs and Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The International Labour Organization was projecting up to 50 million job losses worldwide.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Foreign Affairs and Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Most of our members had only ever known one job their entire lives.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Foreign Affairs and Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: On the workers' last day, we arranged for special buses to take them immediately to the National Trades Union Congress' (NTUC's) Employment and Employability Institute (e2i).

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Foreign Affairs and Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: I went early to receive my brothers and sisters.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Foreign Affairs and Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We wanted them to know that the union would walk this journey together with them and they were not alone.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Foreign Affairs and Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We briefed our members about the union's assistance package, e2i colleagues set up rows of interview counters for everyone who needed help.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Foreign Affairs and Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: They could get face-to-face consultations and follow-up support on the spot.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Foreign Affairs and Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Most of our members found new jobs and continued to provide for their families.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Foreign Affairs and Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In subsequent Chinese New Years, we could still get together to tell stories of children and grandchildren doing well.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Foreign Affairs and Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: My brothers and sisters have lost their old jobs.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Foreign Affairs and Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: But through new jobs, they kept their livelihoods, and their dignity.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Foreign Affairs and Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Whatever our political persuasion, we can all agree on the need for protection against unemployment.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Foreign Affairs and Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: But how we do it is important, and the experience of other countries should give us caution.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Foreign Affairs and Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: None of these is intended, of course, but it could happen.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Foreign Affairs and Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We must try to do it right in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Foreign Affairs and Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We grow the economy to create more good jobs.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Foreign Affairs and Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Even in tough times, Singaporeans want to feel the sense of dignity and pride that comes from standing on one's own feet.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Foreign Affairs and Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: I saw it in 2009 in the eyes of my retrenched brothers and sisters whom we helped get new jobs.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Foreign Affairs and Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: And today, each time a fellow Singaporean gets a new job through our employment support programmes, we see it again.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Foreign Affairs and Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Let us stay focused on making our employment support programmes the best that they can be for all Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Mr Patrick Tay, do you want to ask something?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Would having this suggested insurance not make it even harder for unions to negotiate for better and higher retrenchment packages?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Second, Assoc Prof Daniel Goh suggested insurance is for payout during redundancies, and not unemployment.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: As Director of Legal Services at NTUC, I have come across in these past 15 years, many cases of workers who are unemployed, not just because of redundancy but because of termination, job loss, job fit.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: And his proposal suggests that all these are excluded.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: Again, this is the "either-or" fallacy that I have been speaking about.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: I have already paid my dues to society." But my take is that in our society, in our tripartite stable industrial relations situation, which is underpinned by a certain kind of moral economy, that the unions have a certain kind of moral suasion and the Government, too, that has a hold on employers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: They will not just easily let go of retrenchment benefits just because we have a redundancy insurance.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: If we make it clear to them that redundancy insurance is really workers looking out for fellow workers, it does not replace the retrenchment benefits and the kind of duties that are owed to workers by the employers when they have to lay off staff for whatever reason.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: Of course, there are terminations due to dismissals, due to poor performance, and that would be excluded.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: It is really about redundancy as defined by MOM.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: The time allowed for the proceedings has expired.
